title: Personae: The Collected Poems of Ezra Pound
description: Pound's collected shorter poems to 1926: the troubadour translations, the imagist lyrics and the satires.
plot_or_argument: The volume gathers Pound's shorter poems from 1908 to 1926: the Provençal and Italian translations, the imagist lyrics of Ripostes and Lustra, the Chinese versions of Cathay, the satires and the Mauberley sequence.
narrative_structure: Collected shorter poems arranged by volume of first publication.
historical_context: The London and Paris of the 1910s and 1920s, and the whole range of Pound's early experiments in translation and form.
literary_significance: Personae is the essential single volume of Pound's shorter poetry: it made the case for translation as original composition and gathered the imagist lyrics that taught the century to write free verse.

title: Sea Garden
description: The purest book of Imagism: the sea, the shore, the garden and the mineral world, in the hardest English free verse.
plot_or_argument: The poems — 'Sea Rose', 'The Helmsman', 'Mid-day', 'Garden', 'Sea Lily', 'The Cliff Temple' — are short, hard, unrhymed lyrics of shells, salt, stone and petals, in which the natural world is presented as a set of exact and severe objects and the speaking voice is barely present.
narrative_structure: Thirty-eight short poems, mostly of a few lines, in free verse.
historical_context: The Imagist programme of 1912–14, the Greek lyric (Sappho), and the London little magazines in which the poems first appeared.
literary_significance: Sea Garden is the founding book of Imagism and the purest body of free verse in English: its crystalline images and refusal of rhetoric made it the model for the modern short poem and established H. D. as the finest poet of the movement.

title: Trilogy
description: The great poem of the London Blitz and one of the major long poems of the century: war, resurrection, the female divine and the making of a poet out of the ruins.
plot_or_argument: The three books — 'The Walls Do Not Fall' (1944), 'Tribute to the Angels' (1945) and 'The Flowering of the Rod' (1946) — begin among the ruins of London under bombardment and move through a meditation on the poet's craft, a vision of the angels and the Lady, and the legend of Mary Magdalene and the alabaster jar, arriving at a vision of resurrection.
narrative_structure: Three books of three parts each, in free verse and short lyrics.
principal_characters: The poet; the angels; the Lady; Mary Magdalene
historical_context: The London Blitz of 1940–41, the Second World War, H. D.'s analysis with Freud, and her study of the Gnostic and Hermetic traditions.
literary_significance: Trilogy is one of the great long poems of the period and the founding work of the modernist woman's epic: it turned the Blitz into a vision of resurrection and made the female divine the centre of a modernist poem.

title: North of Boston
description: The book that made Frost: blank-verse dialogues of New England farm life, and the sound of actual speech in American poetry.
plot_or_argument: The collection opens with 'Mending Wall' and contains 'The Death of the Hired Man', 'Home Burial', 'After Apple-Picking', 'The Wood-Pile' and 'A Servant to Servants' — dramatic dialogues and narratives of New England farm life, in which the speakers reveal more than they know.
narrative_structure: Seventeen poems, mostly blank-verse dialogues and narratives.
principal_characters: Silas; Warren; Mary; Amy; the hired man
historical_context: The New Hampshire and Massachusetts farmland of Frost's years at Derry, and the England of 1912–15 where the book was first published.
literary_significance: North of Boston is the book that made Frost and the founding collection of the American dramatic lyric: its blank-verse dialogues brought the sound of actual speech into American poetry, and 'The Death of the Hired Man' and 'Home Burial' are among the greatest narrative poems in the language.

title: Mountain Interval
description: The collection that gave America its most quoted poem: 'The Road Not Taken' and the New England hill farm.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Road Not Taken', 'Birches', 'An Old Man's Winter Night', 'A Time to Talk', 'In the Home Stretch' and 'The Sound of the Trees' — lyrics and dialogues of rural New England.
narrative_structure: Twenty poems, several of them blank-verse dialogues.
historical_context: The New England hill farms, the First World War, and Frost's return to America in 1915.
literary_significance: Mountain Interval gave American poetry its most quoted poem and Frost his popular fame: 'The Road Not Taken' has been misread as a celebration of individual choice for a century, and 'Birches' is one of the best-loved lyrics in the language.

title: New Hampshire
description: The collection that won Frost the first of his four Pulitzer Prizes, and the long title poem of the New England farmer.
plot_or_argument: The book opens with the long title poem, a meditation on the state and its people, and contains 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening', 'Fire and Ice', 'Nothing Gold Can Stay', 'Fragmentary Blue' and 'The Need of Being Versed in Country Things'.
narrative_structure: Forty-five poems, led by the long title poem in blank verse.
literary_form: Poetry collection (with the long poem 'New Hampshire')
historical_context: The New England farm and village of the 1920s, and Frost's position as the country's most honoured poet.
literary_significance: New Hampshire won Frost the first of his four Pulitzer Prizes: it contains 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening' — perhaps the most quoted American poem — and established the late manner of the country poems.

title: Harmonium
description: The most gorgeous first book in American poetry: 'Sunday Morning', the Florida sun and the imagination making its world.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'Sunday Morning', 'The Emperor of Ice-Cream', 'Anecdote of the Jar', 'Peter Quince at the Clavier', 'Le Monocle de Mon Oncle', 'Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird' and 'The Comedian as the Letter C' — poems of the imagination, the body, the weather and the made thing.
narrative_structure: Sixty-seven poems in free and blank verse, from epigrams to long meditations.
historical_context: The imagination's response to the death of the gods, the Florida landscape of Stevens's travels, and the aesthetics of the 1910s.
literary_significance: Harmonium is the greatest first book in American poetry and the founding collection of the American philosophical lyric: 'Sunday Morning' and 'Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird' are permanent, and its sumptuous surface established the imagination as the century's great poetic subject.

title: The Man with the Blue Guitar
description: Stevens's central long poem: the guitar, the blue, and the imagination's argument with reality.
plot_or_argument: The thirty-three cantos of the title poem take Picasso's painting as the figure of the poet whose instrument transforms the world, and the collection's shorter poems — 'The Idea of Order at Key West', 'A Postcard from the Volcano', 'The Pleasures of Merely Circulating' — extend the argument about imagination and reality.
narrative_structure: A long title poem in thirty-three cantos, with a group of shorter lyrics.
principal_characters: The guitarist; the poet; Ramon Fernandez
literary_form: Poetry collection (long title poem and thirty-three lyrics)
historical_context: The Depression and the political pressures of the 1930s, which Stevens answered with a poetry of the imagination rather than of politics.
literary_significance: The Man with the Blue Guitar is the central long poem of Stevens's middle period and the fullest statement of his aesthetic: it is the period's great poem about the relation of art to reality, and 'The Idea of Order at Key West' is among the finest American poems of the century.

title: Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction
description: Stevens's greatest long poem: it must be abstract, it must change, it must give pleasure.
plot_or_argument: The poem's three parts — 'It Must Be Abstract', 'It Must Change' and 'It Must Give Pleasure' — argue for a poetry that replaces the dead gods with a fiction adequate to the modern world, and the sequence closes with the 'fat girl' and the 'ephebe' in the sun.
narrative_structure: Three parts of ten cantos each, in tercets and quatrains.
principal_characters: The ephebe; the canon Aspirin; Nanzia Nunzio; the major man
historical_context: The war years of 1941–42, the death of the gods, and Stevens's mature aesthetic philosophy.
literary_significance: Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction is Stevens's greatest long poem and the central American philosophical poem of the century: its three propositions make the case for the imagination as the modern equivalent of belief.

title: Spring and All
description: The most radical American book of the period: poems and prose manifestos of the imagination, including 'The Red Wheelbarrow'.
plot_or_argument: The book alternates between prose chapters arguing for the primacy of the imagination and short poems that demonstrate it — 'By the road to the contagious hospital', 'The Red Wheelbarrow', 'To Elsie', 'Spring and All' — and ends with the declaration that the imagination is the only reality.
narrative_structure: Twenty-seven sections alternating prose chapters and poems.
literary_form: Poetry collection with prose (published in Paris by Contact Editions)
historical_context: The New Jersey of Williams's medical practice, the Armory Show and the new American art of the 1910s, and the Imagist and Dadaist movements.
literary_significance: Spring and All is the most radical American book of the period: its mixture of manifesto and poem, its plain American idiom and its insistence on things made it the founding text of the American objectivist tradition, and 'The Red Wheelbarrow' is the most discussed short poem in American literature.

title: Paterson
description: The great American long poem of place: a New Jersey city, a doctor, and the search for a language in which things can be said.
plot_or_argument: The poem follows the city of Paterson and its river, its falls and its people, and the figure of the doctor-poet who walks it; it assembles letters, documents, newspaper cuttings and lyric passages into a single work about the American place and the American idiom.
narrative_structure: Five books, each in three parts, mixing lyric, letter and document.
principal_characters: The doctor; Paterson; the river; the falls
historical_context: The industrial city of Paterson, New Jersey, and its history; the America of the 1940s and 1950s; and Williams's own medical practice among its people.
literary_significance: Paterson is the great American long poem after The Waste Land and the founding work of the American objectivist epic: it made a single American city the subject of a modernist long poem.

title: Poems (Moore, 1921)
description: Moore's first collection, published by her friends: the syllabic stanza, the menagerie and the exact eye.
plot_or_argument: The collection — published by the Egoist Press in London — contains 'The Fish', 'A Grave', 'Poetry', 'To a Steam Roller' and 'The Monkeys', the poems that established her syllabic stanza and exact zoological observation.
narrative_structure: Twenty-four poems in syllabic stanzas with internal rhyme.
literary_form: Poetry collection (published by H.D. and Bryher without the poet's knowledge)
historical_context: The New York and London of the little magazines, the Imagist movement, and the exact observation of the natural world.
literary_significance: Moore's Poems is the founding collection of the American syllabic lyric: its publication without her knowledge by H.D. and Bryher is one of the period's great acts of literary friendship.

title: Observations
description: Moore's second collection, the one that made her reputation: 'The Fish', 'A Grave', 'Poetry' and the syllabic stanza perfected.
plot_or_argument: The collection gathers Moore's poems of 1921–24, including 'The Fish', 'A Grave', 'Poetry', 'The Monkeys', 'An Octopus' and 'Sea Unicorns and Land Unicorns', in her characteristic syllabic stanzas.
narrative_structure: Fifty-three poems in syllabic stanzas.
historical_context: The New York of the 1920s, the Dial circle, and the new American poetry of the little magazines.
literary_significance: Observations is the collection that established Moore as a major American poet: its syllabic stanzas and its exact observation made her the most distinctive technician of American modernism.

title: Tulips and Chimneys
description: Cummings's first collection: the typographic lyric, the love poem and the satire of the modern state.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'in Just-spring', 'the Cambridge ladies who live in furnished souls', 'Thy fingers make early flowers of', 'Buffalo Bill's defunct' and 'next to of course god america i' — love lyrics, satires and the first full display of Cummings's typographic method.
narrative_structure: Seventy-three poems, including sonnets, songs and typographic experiments.
historical_context: The Cambridge and Greenwich Village of the 1910s, the First World War, and the new art movements of the period.
literary_significance: Tulips and Chimneys introduced the typographic poem to English and established Cummings as the most popular experimental poet of the century: its lowercase 'i', its broken words and its parenthesis made the printed page part of the poem.

title: The Bridge
description: The great American epic of the Brooklyn Bridge: the myth of America, the machine and the poetic imagination.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins with 'Proem: To Brooklyn Bridge' and moves through Columbus, Pocahontas, the subway, the Mississippi riverboat, the tramp, the sailor and the film comedians, ending with 'Atlantis' and a vision of the bridge as the symbol of American possibility and of the poet's own aspiration.
narrative_structure: Fifteen sections in a symphonic structure, from 'Ave Maria' to 'Atlantis'.
principal_characters: Columbus; Pocahontas; Rip Van Winkle; the sailor; the poet
historical_context: The Brooklyn Bridge, New York in the 1920s, the American past from Columbus to the frontier, and Crane's reading of Whitman and Eliot.
literary_significance: The Bridge is the great American epic poem of the period and the most ambitious answer to The Waste Land: it attempted to give America a mythic poem of its own, and its fusion of the machine, the past and the imagination made it the most beautiful long poem of American modernism.

title: 1914 and Other Poems
description: The five 1914 sonnets and the Georgian lyrics of the poet who became the emblem of the war's first year.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains the five war sonnets of 1914 — 'Peace', 'Safety', 'The Dead' (two), 'The Soldier' — together with the earlier Georgian lyrics, 'The Old Vicarage, Grantchester', 'The Great Lover' and the South Seas poems.
narrative_structure: A posthumous collection of lyrics and the five war sonnets.
historical_context: The first year of the First World War, Brooke's service with the Royal Naval Division, and his death on the hospital ship off Skyros in April 1915, which made the book a national event.
literary_significance: 1914 and Other Poems gave the war its rhetoric of sacrifice: 'The Soldier' — 'some corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England' — is one of the most famous English poems of the century, and the book's posthumous publication made Brooke the myth of the golden generation.

title: The Listeners and Other Poems
description: The book that made de la Mare famous: 'The Listeners', 'Silver' and the English supernatural lyric.
plot_or_argument: The title poem, 'The Listeners', is the most famous English ghost poem — the traveller who knocks at the moonlit door and is answered only by silence and the listening phantoms; the collection also contains 'Silver', 'The Song of the Mad Prince', 'Old Susan' and 'The Quince Tree'.
narrative_structure: A collection of lyrics in varied stanza forms, led by the title poem.
principal_characters: The traveller; the listeners; the phantom listeners
historical_context: The English countryside and the ghost-story tradition of the period; de la Mare's years as an oil-company clerk writing in the evenings.
literary_significance: The Listeners and Other Poems made de la Mare famous and established the English supernatural lyric as a modern form: 'The Listeners' is the most famous ghost poem in the language and 'Silver' one of the best-loved short poems of the century.

title: Peacock Pie
description: The finest book of children's verse of the century: 'The Quince Tree', 'Off the Ground' and the world seen from a child's height.
plot_or_argument: The collection's poems — 'The Horseman', 'Off the Ground', 'The Cupboard', 'The Quartette', 'Some One', 'The Ruin', 'The Window' — are songs and riddles of the nursery, the farmyard, the ghost and the dream, written with a perfect ear for the child's cadence.
narrative_structure: Over eighty short poems and songs for children.
historical_context: The Edwardian nursery, the English countryside, and the golden age of the illustrated children's book.
literary_significance: Peacock Pie is the finest book of children's verse of the period and one of the permanent children's books in English: its songs, riddles and ghosts have been read to children for a century, and it is the equal in its kind of the Alice books.

title: The Collected Poems of Edward Thomas
description: The 140 poems Thomas wrote in three years: the finest English nature poetry of the century and the quietest war poetry.
plot_or_argument: The poems — 'Adlestrop', 'The Owl', 'Rain', 'Old Man', 'Words', 'Lights Out', 'Aspens', 'The Glory', 'February Afternoon' — record the English countryside, the road, the hedge, the bird and the coming of the war, in a plain, unemphatic verse that stops rather than concludes.
narrative_structure: One hundred and forty poems in plain rhymed and unrhymed verse.
historical_context: The English countryside of Kent, Hampshire and Wiltshire; the First World War, which Thomas enlisted in 1915 to escape his own depression, and his death at Arras on 9 April 1917.
literary_significance: Thomas's Collected Poems is the finest body of English nature poetry of the century and among the greatest war poetry: in three years he wrote 140 poems, 'Adlestrop' and 'Rain' are permanent, and his prose founded the modern nature essay.

title: The Old Huntsman and Other Poems
description: The book that made Sassoon the war's great satirist: 'The Old Huntsman', 'The Hero' and the first poems of protest.
plot_or_argument: The collection opens with the long title poem on the English hunting field and turns in its second half to the war: 'The Hero', 'They', 'Base Details', 'The General' and 'The Death-Bed', the satirical poems that made Sassoon the spokesman of the soldiers' anger.
narrative_structure: A collection in two halves: the English poems and the war poems.
principal_characters: The old huntsman; the major; the general; the bishop
historical_context: The First World War, the Royal Welch Fusiliers, and Sassoon's own experience of the trenches and of the protest that sent him to Craiglockhart.
literary_significance: The Old Huntsman gave the war its most effective satirical voice: 'Base Details' and 'The General' are the sharpest anti-war poems in English, and the collection's contrast between the English hunting field and the Western Front is one of the period's great structures.
